meta.titre: States of Matter: particles, changes of state and heating curves
meta.sous_theme: Kinetic theory and changes of state

sections.contenu_markdown: A bottle of cooking gas in a kitchen in Bafoussam holds a gas under pressure, the water in the pot becomes steam when it boils, and the ice block sold at the roadside slowly melts in the sun. The same substance can be solid, liquid or gas, depending on temperature and pressure. Understanding how the particles are arranged and how they move explains why ice floats, why smells spread across a room and why steam burns. Questions in the GCE O/L paper ask you to name the changes of state, to describe the particles in each state and to interpret heating curves.

items: All matter is made of tiny particles (atoms, molecules or ions).
Heating a substance gives its particles more energy.
Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius with a thermometer.

sections.titre: The three states of matter and the changes between them
sections.contenu_markdown:
The **kinetic theory** says that matter is made of particles that are always moving, and the state depends on how strongly the particles attract one another compared with how much energy they have.

| | Solid | Liquid | Gas |
|---|---|---|---|
| Arrangement | closely packed in a regular pattern | closely packed, irregular | far apart, random |
| Movement | vibrate about fixed positions | slide past one another | move quickly in all directions |
| Forces between particles | strong | weaker | very weak |
| Shape | fixed | shape of the container | fills the container |
| Volume | fixed | fixed | not fixed |
| Compressible | no | almost not | yes |

**Changes of state** (the arrows show the direction):

| Change | Name | Energy |
|---|---|---|
| solid to liquid | melting | absorbed |
| liquid to solid | freezing (solidifying) | released |
| liquid to gas | boiling or evaporation | absorbed |
| gas to liquid | condensation | released |
| solid to gas | sublimation | absorbed |

Some substances, such as solid carbon dioxide (dry ice), iodine and ammonium chloride, change straight from solid to gas on heating, and the gas turns directly back into a solid on cooling.

**Evaporation** happens at the surface of a liquid at any temperature, whereas **boiling** happens throughout the liquid at one fixed temperature, the boiling point. The melting point and boiling point of a pure substance are fixed; pure water melts at 0 $^\circ$C and boils at 100 $^\circ$C.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a table or graph of temperature against time is given.
variantes.contenu_markdown: When a solid is heated steadily the temperature rises, stays constant while it melts, rises again as a liquid, stays constant while it boils, then rises as a gas. During the flat parts, the energy supplied is used to **overcome the forces between particles**, not to raise the temperature. A pure substance gives flat parts at its melting point and boiling point; an impure substance melts over a range of temperatures.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a smell, colour or gas spreads through a space.
variantes.contenu_markdown: **Diffusion** is the spreading of particles from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration because of their random motion. It is fastest in gases, slow in liquids and negligible in solids. It is faster at a higher temperature. Lighter particles diffuse faster than heavier ones. Example: cotton wool soaked in ammonia at one end of a glass tube and cotton wool soaked in hydrochloric acid at the other end give a white ring of ammonium chloride, $\mathrm{NH_{3}} + \mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH_{4}Cl}$. The ring forms closer to the hydrochloric acid end because hydrogen chloride (relative molecular mass 36.5) diffuses more slowly than ammonia (relative molecular mass 17).

sections.enonce_markdown:
A pure solid is heated steadily and its temperature is read every 2 minutes.

| Time (min) | Temperature ($^\circ$C) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 20 |
| 2 | 40 |
| 4 | 60 |
| 6 | 60 |
| 8 | 60 |
| 10 | 90 |
| 12 | 120 |
| 14 | 150 |
| 16 | 150 |
| 18 | 150 |

(a) Find the melting point and the boiling point. (b) What is the state of the substance at 2 minutes and at 12 minutes? (c) What is present at 5 minutes? (d) Explain why the temperature does not rise between 4 and 8 minutes.

etapes.action: Find the flat parts of the table.
etapes.justification: A pure substance has constant temperature while it changes state.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The temperature is constant at $60\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (4 to 8 minutes) and at $150\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (14 to 18 minutes).

etapes.action: Name the melting and boiling points.
etapes.justification: The first flat part is melting; the second is boiling.

etapes.action: State the states at 2 and 12 minutes.
etapes.justification: Compare the temperature with the melting and boiling points.
etapes.resultat_markdown: At 2 minutes the temperature $(40\ ^\circ\mathrm{C})$ is below $60\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so it is a **solid**. At 12 minutes it is $120\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, between the two points, so it is a **liquid**.

etapes.action: Say what is present at 5 minutes.
etapes.justification: The temperature is at the melting point, so melting is in progress.
Energy is still being supplied but the temperature is constant.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The energy is used to overcome the forces holding the particles in the solid, so the particles can move apart and slide past each other; the energy does not increase the kinetic energy, so the temperature stays at $60\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The substance melts at $60\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and boils at $150\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$; it is solid at 2 minutes, liquid at 12 minutes, and the flat parts show energy being used to change state.

items.erreur_markdown: "Boiling and evaporation are the same thing."
items.pourquoi_faux: Evaporation occurs only at the surface and at any temperature below the boiling point; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at the boiling point.
items.correction_markdown: Evaporation: surface, any temperature. Boiling: whole liquid, fixed boiling point, bubbles of vapour.

items.erreur_markdown: "When a solid melts, its particles become bigger."
items.pourquoi_faux: The particles themselves do not change size or change into something else. Only their arrangement and movement change.
items.correction_markdown: When a solid melts, the particles stay the same size, but they leave their fixed positions and slide past one another.

items.erreur_markdown: "The temperature keeps rising while a pure solid melts."
items.pourquoi_faux: During a change of state the temperature of a pure substance stays constant. The energy supplied breaks the forces between particles.
items.correction_markdown: The temperature is constant at the melting point until all the solid has melted.

items.erreur_markdown: "Sublimation is the change from liquid to gas."
items.pourquoi_faux: That change is boiling or evaporation. Sublimation skips the liquid stage and goes from solid directly to gas.
items.correction_markdown: Sublimation: solid $\rightarrow$ gas (for example solid carbon dioxide or iodine).

items.erreur_markdown: "Gases have no mass, so they cannot be weighed."
items.pourquoi_faux: Gas particles are far apart, but they still have mass. Gases have a low density, not zero mass.
items.correction_markdown: A gas has mass; for example, a full gas cylinder is heavier than an empty one.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the change of state that takes place in each case. (a) Ice blocks change into water on a hot day. (b) Water vapour from a boiling pot forms drops on a cold lid. (c) Water in a tray is placed in a freezer. (d) A lump of solid iodine, when heated gently, changes into purple vapour without becoming a liquid. (e) State one difference between the particles in a liquid and the particles in a gas.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Melting**. (b) **Condensation**. (c) **Freezing** (solidifying). (d) **Sublimation**.

(e) In a liquid the particles are close together and slide past each other; in a gas they are far apart and move quickly and randomly, with almost no attraction between them.

items.enonce_markdown:
Cotton wool soaked in concentrated ammonia solution is placed at one end of a long dry glass tube, and cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrochloric acid is placed at the other end. Both ends are closed with stoppers. After a few minutes, a white ring forms inside the tube.

(a) Name the white solid and write the equation for its formation. (b) Explain, using the kinetic theory, how the ammonia and hydrogen chloride reach each other. (c) The ring forms nearer to the hydrochloric acid end. Explain why, using the relative molecular masses (ammonia 17, hydrogen chloride 36.5). (d) How would the ring position change if the whole tube were warmed?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Ammonium chloride**: $\mathrm{NH_{3}} + \mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH_{4}Cl}$.

(b) Both gases are made of particles that move randomly and quickly, so they spread out by **diffusion** until they meet.

(c) Ammonia particles are lighter (17 against 36.5), so they move faster and cover a longer distance in the same time. The gases meet closer to the end where the slower hydrogen chloride started, which is the hydrochloric acid end.

(d) The ring would form **sooner**, because both gases move faster; its position (nearer the hydrochloric acid end) would stay about the same.

items.enonce_markdown:
The melting and boiling points of four substances are given.

| Substance | P | Q | R | S |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Melting point ($^\circ$C) | $-7$ | 801 | $-100$ | 44 |
| Boiling point ($^\circ$C) | 59 | 1413 | $-35$ | 280 |

(a) State the physical state of each substance at 25 $^\circ$C. (b) State the physical state of each substance at 100 $^\circ$C. (c) Which substance would be a solid at 25 $^\circ$C but a liquid at 100 $^\circ$C? (d) Which substance is a gas at 100 $^\circ$C but a solid at $-80\ ^\circ$C? Explain.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) At 25 $^\circ$C: **P is a liquid** (between $-7$ and 59), **Q is a solid** (below 801), **R is a gas** (above $-35$), **S is a solid** (below 44).

(b) At 100 $^\circ$C: **P is a gas** (above 59), **Q is a solid**, **R is a gas**, **S is a liquid** (between 44 and 280).

(c) **S**.

(d) **P**. It is a gas at 100 $^\circ$C (above 59 $^\circ$C), and at $-80\ ^\circ$C it is below its melting point ($-7\ ^\circ$C), so it is a solid. Q is a solid at both temperatures, S is a liquid at 100 $^\circ$C, and R is a gas at 100 $^\circ$C but only a liquid at $-80\ ^\circ$C (between $-100$ and $-35$).

items_markdown: In a solid the particles vibrate in fixed positions; in a liquid they slide past each other; in a gas they are far apart and move quickly and randomly.
Melting, freezing, boiling or evaporation, condensation and sublimation are the names of the changes of state.
During a change of state the temperature of a pure substance stays constant because the energy goes into overcoming forces between particles.
Evaporation is a surface process at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point.
Diffusion shows that particles move; it is faster for gases, at higher temperature, and for lighter particles.
